svg.title: LLMD on ZML
svg.desc: The serving APIs connect clients to the LLMD engine. The DeepSeek V4.1-Flash example expands a decoder layer. A matrix shows kernel implementations for each platform. ZML compiles and executes tensor programs through PJRT plugins.

g.desc: LLMD exposes inference APIs and coordinates work in its serving engine. The engine runs model logic written in Zig on ZML.
Applications and agents send HTTP requests to LLMD. Chat clients can receive generated content as a stream.
The OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint accepts messages and returns a completion. Clients can also stream the generated content.
The embeddings endpoint converts input text into a vector. The model output is pooled on the device.
The Decision endpoint evaluates typed questions against one shared state. Questions can depend on earlier answers.
Prometheus metrics expose service behavior. Crash reports provide information for investigating failures.
The engine prepares input, schedules batches and manages cached attention state. It runs the model and processes its output for clients.
The Jinja2 engine in Zig formats conversation messages into the prompt expected by the selected chat model.
Tokenizers turn input text into token IDs. The diagram lists BPE, WordPiece and SentencePiece.
Output parsers interpret generated content such as reasoning traces and tool calls.
The scheduler combines work from active requests into batches. Chunked prefill lets it process a prompt in pieces.
The engine stores attention keys and values in pages. Requests with a common prefix can reuse cached state.
A drafter proposes candidate tokens for the target model to verify. The diagram names DSpark, DFlash and DSpine.
The host prepares the next execution step while the device runs the current one.
LLMD can divide tensors or experts across devices, or distribute inputs across model replicas.
Weights can be fused, stacked or rearranged into the layout required by the selected kernel. The diagram includes FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4.
DeepSeek V4.1-Flash is the worked example. Its Zig definition connects token embeddings, repeated decoder layers, an output head and sampling.
The embedding stage looks up a vector for each token ID and passes those vectors to the decoder.
The decoder layers repeat through the model. The expanded layer shows Engram on selected layers, sparse MLA attention and mixture of experts.
The language model head maps the decoder output to scores over the token vocabulary.
The sampler uses the model’s output scores to select tokens for generation.
The example includes a DSpark drafter that uses one decoder layer for speculative decoding.
On selected layers, the host computes n-gram hashes. Engram looks up values in host-pinned tables and combines them with the residual through a gate.

Sparse MLA forms latent query and key/value projections, applies YaRN rotary embeddings and compresses KV state. An indexer selects candidates for sliding-window and sparse attention; attention sinks and a grouped output projection complete the block.
A router chooses top-k MXFP4 experts. The model also has a shared expert and can distribute experts across devices.
The example mixes residual streams before and after the attention and expert computations.

text.tspan: residual streams mixed before and after attention and experts

g.desc: The example keeps window keys and values in FP8, compressed keys and values in FP4, and indexer keys in FP4.
The matrix maps five operation families to eight platforms. Solid cells mark custom kernels, dashed cells mark portable StableHLO, and a dash means no implementation is specified in the diagram.
g.text: operations pick the best kernel per platform

g.desc: Attention covers implementations such as MLA and grouped-query attention. The row shows the implementation named for each platform.
The indexer selects candidates for sparse attention. The example matrix includes DSA and QSA.
The Gated DeltaNet row lists custom kernels on six platforms. The source leaves the Trainium and CPU entries unspecified.
Mixture-of-experts operations can use a platform-specific kernel or portable StableHLO as shown for each target.
These operations mix residual streams. The diagram gives custom implementations for NVIDIA and AMD and portable StableHLO for the other targets.
ZML connects Zig tensor operations, kernel implementations and model weights with the compiler and the selected backend’s runtime.
The runtime launches compiled executables asynchronously with device buffers holding model parameters and inputs.
Specialized kernels written in these languages can be embedded in the model graph alongside portable operations.
The compiler generates MLIR from Zig model code, with one program per shape bucket. The diagram identifies StableHLO, Shardy (sdy) and func dialects.
Model authors express tensor operations in Zig, including matrix multiplication, gather, scan and sort.
ZML can load tensors from disk or remote sources such as Hugging Face, S3, GCS and HTTP. DMA transfers data between host and device.
ZML uses the PJRT C API to compile programs, transfer buffers and execute through a platform plugin.
g.text: one plugin interface for every platform

g.desc: A device mesh has named axes. Tensor sharding declarations tell XLA how to partition the computation across that mesh.
The diagram lists eight framework targets reached through PJRT plugins and custom kernel languages. Published LLMD launch combinations are listed in Model compatibility.
The NVIDIA target uses CUDA. The schematic lists CuTe, CUDA Tile and Triton for custom kernels.
The AMD target uses ROCm. The schematic lists FlyDSL and Triton for custom kernels.
The Google TPU target uses libtpu, with Mosaic for custom kernels.
The AWS Trainium target uses Neuron, with NKI for custom kernels.
The Intel target uses oneAPI, with Triton for custom kernels.
The Apple target uses Metal for the runtime and for custom GPU kernels.
The Furiosa target uses the Furiosa SDK, with TCL for custom kernels.
The schematic includes x86 and Arm CPUs as framework targets.
